title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.1 Prepare Timeline Data


Code
timeline_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  mutate(
    source_group = case_when(
      is_public ~ "Public Post",
      channel == "one_on_one_chat" ~ "One-on-One Chat",
      channel == "comms_huddle" ~ "Comms Huddle",
      TRUE ~ "Other Internal Communication"
    ),
    short_content = str_trunc(content, width = 120)
  ) %>%
  arrange(timestamp)




Code
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")

timeline_data <- timeline_data %>%
  mutate(
    breach_window = case_when(
      timestamp < breach_time ~ "Before 5:00 PM Breach",
      timestamp >= breach_time & timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~ "5:00–6:00 PM Embargo Breach Window",
      timestamp >= embargo_lift_time ~ "After 6:00 PM Embargo Lift"
    )
  )

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.2 Overall Communication Timeline


Code
ggplot(
  timeline_data,
  aes(
    x = timestamp,
    y = source_group,
    color = source_group
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Communication Timeline Before the Breach",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one communication record",
    x = "Timestamp",
    y = "Communication Type",
    color = "Communication Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









The timeline indicates that TenantThread’s communication activity continued throughout the two-week period, with Comms Huddle, One-on-One Chat, and Public Posts appearing repeatedly. This suggests that public-facing communication occurred alongside ongoing internal discussion rather than as a single isolated event. “Other Internal Communication” is much less frequent and appears only on selected dates. The clustering of records near the end of the period suggests that later sections should examine whether communication density, merger-related content, or urgency signals increased closer to the breach.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.3 Daily Communication Volume


Code
daily_volume <- timeline_data %>%
  count(date, source_group)

ggplot(
  daily_volume,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = n,
    fill = source_group
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Communication Volume",
    subtitle = "Number of communication records by day and communication type",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Communications",
    fill = "Communication Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









Daily communication volume remains relatively stable during most of the two-week period, but rises sharply in early June. The final spike reaches almost 500 communication records, far above the earlier daily levels. Importantly, this increase includes multiple communication types rather than only public posts, suggesting a broader escalation of internal and external communication activity. This pattern provides an initial indication that the breach occurred during a high-pressure communication period, which will be examined further in the system pressure analysis.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.4 Merger-Related Communication Timeline


Code
merger_spread_heatmap <- timeline_data %>%
  filter(contains_merger == TRUE) %>%
  count(date, agent_label, name = "merger_count")

ggplot(
  merger_spread_heatmap,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = agent_label,
    fill = merger_count
  )
) +
  geom_tile(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = ifelse(merger_count > 0, merger_count, "")),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "white",
    high = "darkblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Spread of Merger-Related Communication Across Agents",
    subtitle = "Darker cells indicate more merger-related communications by agent and date",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Agent",
    fill = "Merger Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1)
  )









Merger-related communications are sparse in the earlier period but become much more concentrated near early June. The later cluster involves more agents, including Legal, PR, Social Manager, PR Intern, Judge, and Intern agents. This suggests that merger-related information became more widely circulated close to the breach period, which makes the later information-flow and public-post comparison especially important.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.5 Key Signal Trends Over Time


Code

title: Take-Home_Ex02
section: 4.6 Breach Window Signal Intensity on June 5
text:
4.6 Breach Window Signal Intensity on June 5
This visual zooms into June 5, 2046, the day of the inappropriate release. The vertical reference lines mark the approximate breach time at 5:00 PM and the formal embargo lift at 6:00 PM. This allows the analysis to separate behavior before the breach, during the embargo breach window, and after the embargo was formally lifted.


Code
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")

breach_day_data <- timeline_data %>%
  filter(date == as_date("2046-06-05")) %>%
  mutate(
    breach_phase = case_when(
      timestamp < breach_time ~ "Before 5:00 PM",
      timestamp >= breach_time & timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~ "5:00–6:00 PM Breach Window",
      timestamp >= embargo_lift_time ~ "After 6:00 PM Embargo Lift"
    ),
    breach_phase = factor(
      breach_phase,
      levels = c(
        "Before 5:00 PM",
        "5:00–6:00 PM Breach Window",
        "After 6:00 PM Embargo Lift"
      )
    )
  )

day_start <- min(breach_day_data$timestamp, na.rm = TRUE)
day_end <- max(breach_day_data$timestamp, na.rm = TRUE)

phase_duration <- tibble(
  breach_phase = factor(
    c(
      "Before 5:00 PM",
      "5:00–6:00 PM Breach Window",
      "After 6:00 PM Embargo Lift"
    ),
    levels = c(
      "Before 5:00 PM",
      "5:00–6:00 PM Breach Window",
      "After 6:00 PM Embargo Lift"
    )
  ),
  duration_hours = c(
    as.numeric(difftime(breach_time, day_start, units = "hours")),
    1,
    as.numeric(difftime(day_end, embargo_lift_time, units = "hours"))
  )
)

breach_phase_summary <- breach_day_data %>%
  group_by(breach_phase) %>%
  summarise(
    `Public + Merger` = sum(is_public & contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Public Posts` = sum(is_public, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Merger-Related` = sum(contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Confidentiality-Related` = sum(contains_confidential, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Urgency-Related` = sum(contains_urgency, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    phase_duration,
    by = "breach_phase"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      `Public + Merger`,
      `Public Posts`,
      `Merger-Related`,
      `Confidentiality-Related`,
      `Urgency-Related`
    ),
    names_to = "signal_type",
    values_to = "message_count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    intensity_per_hour = message_count / duration_hours,
    signal_type = factor(
      signal_type,
      levels = c(
        "Public + Merger",
        "Public Posts",
        "Merger-Related",
        "Confidentiality-Related",
        "Urgency-Related"
      )
    )
  )

ggplot(
  breach_phase_summary,
  aes(
    x = intensity_per_hour,
    y = signal_type,
    fill = breach_phase
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    width = 0.65
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Breach Window Signal Intensity on June 5",
    subtitle = "Signal counts standardised as messages per hour across key embargo phases",
    x = "Messages per Hour",
    y = "Signal Type",
    fill = "Breach Phase"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









The chart shows that merger-related and public-merger signals were already present before the 6:00 PM embargo lift. The 5:00–6:00 PM breach window has a clear increase in merger-related and public-facing merger activity, which suggests that embargoed information had started moving into public communication before the authorised release time. After 6:00 PM, all signal types rise further, but the key issue is that public merger-related communication was not zero before the embargo expired.

title: Take-Home_Ex02

title: Take-Home_Ex02
section: 4.8 Slack Screenshot as the Turning Point from Inference to Direct Leakage
text:
4.8 Slack Screenshot as the Turning Point from Inference to Direct Leakage


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(ggrepel)

slack_timeline <- tribble(
  ~time, ~event, ~phase, ~severity,
  "2046-06-05 11:37:00",
  "CivicLoom speculation may overtake the ResidentIQ story before noon",
  "Market inference",
  2,
  "2046-06-05 11:41:00",
  "Legal: internal Slack screenshots are reaching Said-it within 20 minutes",
  "Internal leak",
  4,
  "2046-06-05 11:51:00",
  "Social-Manager: Employee Slack says 'the merger saves all our jobs'",
  "Direct public evidence",
  5,
  "2046-06-05 11:53:00",
  "Legal: Slack leak supports Section 8.1 confidentiality breach argument",
  "Legal breach",
  5,
  "2046-06-05 17:00:00",
  "SaltWind publishes TenantThread-CivicLoom merger story",
  "Public confirmation",
  5
) %>%
  mutate(time = ymd_hms(time))

ggplot(slack_timeline, aes(x = time, y = severity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = event),
    size = 3,
    max.overlaps = Inf,
    label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(2, 4, 5),
    labels = c("Inference", "Internal leak", "Confirmed breach")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Slack Screenshot Escalation Timeline",
    subtitle = "The Slack evidence marks the shift from market inference to direct internal leakage",
    x = "Time on 5 June 2046",
    y = "Disclosure stage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)
  )









This timeline adds event-level evidence to the communication-volume timeline. The earlier part of the crisis was dominated by market inference, including speculation around CivicLoom and ResidentIQ. However, the Slack screenshot changed the nature of the breach. Legal reported that internal Slack screenshots were reaching Said-it within approximately 20 minutes, while Social-Manager later listed an employee Slack post saying “the merger saves all our jobs” as a confirmed public data point. This means the pre-6 PM exposure was not only a product of external speculation; it included direct internal leakage.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
4.9 Key Findings from Timeline Reconstruction

The breach occurred during a clear escalation phase, not during routine communication.
Communication activity remained moderate for most of the two-week period, but surged sharply on June 5. Internal, private, public, and other communication types all increased at the same time, indicating that the organisation had entered crisis communication mode rather than a normal coordination period.
Merger-related information became highly concentrated near the breach window.
The agent-date heatmap shows that merger-related communication was sparse earlier in the period but became highly concentrated on June 5, especially around Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent. This suggests that merger information had moved beyond a narrow legal-control context and was being actively discussed, monitored, and managed across multiple communication spaces.
Urgency, merger, and confidentiality signals intensified together.
The signal escalation heatmap shows a strong concentration of urgency, merger-related, and confidentiality-related signals on June 5. This indicates that the release happened during a period when sensitive merger information, legal risk, and communication pressure were escalating simultaneously.
The Slack screenshot marks the turning point from market inference to direct internal leakage.
Before the formal embargo lift, public discussion was not based only on external speculation or weak signals. The dataset records an employee Slack message stating that “the merger saves all our jobs” appearing on Said-it/r/PropTech, while Legal later described internal Slack screenshots reaching Said-it within about 20 minutes and treated this as a compromised information perimeter. This means the breach included direct internal leakage, not merely public inference.
The 5:00–6:00 PM window is critical because the embargo was still active.
The breach-window comparison shows that public-merger signals were already present before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift. This is direct evidence that embargoed merger information had entered public-facing communication before it was formally authorised.
Pre-embargo merger communication was not limited to private or legal channels.
Before 6:00 PM, merger-related information appeared across internal, private, and public scopes, and across channels including side_huddle, one_on_one_chat, comms_huddle, personal_post, official_post, and anonymous_post. This broad channel distribution shows that the confidentiality boundary had weakened before the official release.
Overall, the timeline evidence supports a mixed leakage pathway rather than a simple system-breakdown explanation.
The inappropriate release appears to have developed in stages. First, market participants and external observers began reconstructing the merger from partial signals. Second, the Slack screenshot introduced direct internal evidence into the public domain. Third, Legal and communication agents shifted toward accelerated disclosure and narrative control. Therefore, the timeline does not support a clean binary conclusion of either deliberate leak or accidental system failure. The stronger interpretation is that an internal confidentiality leak was enabled by system-level control failure and then managed through deliberate post-leak crisis communication.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.1 Agent Communication Composition
This visual examines each agent’s communication composition across public, private, and internal scopes. Instead of only comparing total message counts, the proportional view shows whether an agent was mainly active in internal discussion, one-on-one coordination, or public-facing communication.

agent_scope_composition <- communications_integrated %>%

PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent have the largest public-facing shares, while Judge-Agent has no public communication and is mostly internal/private. Legal, PR, Social Manager, and Platform Trust combine internal discussion with private coordination, suggesting that key operational agents worked across multiple communication spaces.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.3 Reply-Based Message Flow between Agents
This visual uses reply relationships to approximate agent-to-agent communication flow. If one message responds to another message, the original message sender is treated as the source agent, while the replying agent is treated as the target agent.


Code
message_lookup <- communications_integrated %>%
  select(
    responding_to = message_id,
    source_agent = agent_label
  )

reply_flow <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(!is.na(responding_to)) %>%
  left_join(
    message_lookup,
    by = "responding_to"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(source_agent)) %>%
  mutate(
    target_agent = agent_label
  )

agent_flow <- reply_flow %>%
  count(
    source_agent,
    target_agent,
    name = "flow_count"
  ) %>%
  filter(source_agent != target_agent) %>%
  arrange(desc(flow_count)) %>%
  slice_max(flow_count, n = 20) %>%
  mutate(
    flow_id = row_number()
  )

flow_long <- agent_flow %>%
  select(
    flow_id,
    source_agent,
    target_agent,
    flow_count
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(source_agent, target_agent),
    names_to = "flow_side",
    values_to = "agent"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    flow_side = recode(
      flow_side,
      source_agent = "Source Agent",
      target_agent = "Replying Agent"
    ),
    flow_side = factor(
      flow_side,
      levels = c("Source Agent", "Replying Agent")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  flow_long,
  aes(
    x = flow_side,
    y = agent,
    group = flow_id
  )
) +
  geom_line(
    aes(
      linewidth = flow_count,
      colour = flow_count
    ),
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      size = flow_count,
      fill = flow_count
    ),
    shape = 21,
    colour = "grey35",
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_continuous(
    range = c(0.4, 3),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(3, 10),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_colour_gradient(
    low = "lightblue",
    high = "darkblue",
    name = "Reply Count"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "lightblue",
    high = "darkblue",
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Reply-Based Message Flow between Agents",
    subtitle = "Darker and thicker links indicate stronger reply-based communication flow",
    x = "",
    y = "Agent"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









This chart shows that reply-based communication is concentrated around several core agents, especially Legal-Agent, Platform-Trust-Agent, and Social-Manager-Agent. The thickest and darkest links indicate stronger reply flows between these agents, suggesting that they formed the main communication backbone. PR-Agent and PR-Intern-Agent also appear in the reply structure, but with less dominant flow intensity. This helps identify which agents should be examined more closely when tracing sensitive information movement.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.4 Reply-Based Agent Relationship Network
This network visualises reply-based relationships between agents. Each node represents an agent, and each edge represents a reply relationship. Larger nodes indicate agents with more communication records, while thicker edges indicate stronger reply-based interaction between agents.


Code
library(igraph)
library(ggraph)

message_lookup <- communications_integrated %>%
  select(
    responding_to = message_id,
    source_agent = agent_label,
    source_role = agent_role
  )

reply_edges <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(!is.na(responding_to)) %>%
  left_join(
    message_lookup,
    by = "responding_to"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(source_agent)) %>%
  mutate(
    target_agent = agent_label,
    target_role = agent_role
  ) %>%
  filter(source_agent != target_agent) %>%
  count(
    source_agent,
    target_agent,
    name = "reply_count"
  )

agent_nodes <- communications_integrated %>%
  count(
    agent_label,
    agent_role,
    name = "message_count"
  ) %>%
  rename(
    name = agent_label,
    role = agent_role
  )

agent_network <- graph_from_data_frame(
  d = reply_edges,
  vertices = agent_nodes,
  directed = TRUE
)

ggraph(agent_network, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(width = reply_count),
    alpha = 0.35,
    colour = "grey35",
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(2.2, "mm")),
    end_cap = circle(3, "mm")
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(
      size = message_count,
      colour = role
    ),
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = name),
    repel = TRUE,
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.3, 2.2),
    name = "Reply Count"
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(5, 11),
    name = "Message Count"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Reply-Based Agent Relationship Network",
    subtitle = "Node size represents message volume; edge thickness represents reply frequency",
    colour = "Agent Role"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20)
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(
      title = "Agent Role",
      nrow = 2,
      override.aes = list(size = 4)
    ),
    size = guide_legend(
      title = "Message Count",
      nrow = 1
    ),
    edge_width = guide_legend(
      title = "Reply Count",
      nrow = 1
    )
  )









This network shows that Legal-Agent, Platform-Trust-Agent, Social-Manager-Agent, and PR-Agent form the core reply-based communication structure. The largest nodes and thicker links suggest that these agents were central to coordination and information exchange. PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent are less central overall, but they remain connected to the main network, which matters because they also have public-facing communication roles. This structure suggests that sensitive information could move from core internal agents toward public-facing actors through existing reply relationships.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.5 Communication Boundary Bridge Map
This visual identifies which agents operated across internal, private, and public communication spaces. Agents with both high internal activity and visible public-facing activity are especially important for later leak-tracing analysis because they sit closer to the boundary between internal coordination and public communication.


Code
bridge_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  count(agent_label, communication_scope, name = "message_count") %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    total_messages = sum(message_count),
    share = message_count / total_messages
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(agent_label, communication_scope, share, total_messages) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = communication_scope,
    values_from = share,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  rename(
    internal_share = Internal,
    private_share = `Private / One-on-One`,
    public_share = Public
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    bridge_score = private_share + public_share,

    label_x = case_when(
      agent_label == "Platform-Trust-Agent" ~ internal_share + 0.040,
      agent_label == "Judge-Agent" ~ internal_share - 0.050,
      agent_label == "Legal-Agent" ~ internal_share - 0.035,
      agent_label == "PR-Agent" ~ internal_share + 0.030,
      agent_label == "Social-Manager-Agent" ~ internal_share + 0.005,
      agent_label == "PR-Intern-Agent" ~ internal_share - 0.005,
      agent_label == "Intern-Agent" ~ internal_share + 0.005,
      TRUE ~ internal_share
    ),

    label_y = case_when(
      agent_label == "Platform-Trust-Agent" ~ public_share - 0.010,
      agent_label == "Judge-Agent" ~ public_share + 0.018,
      agent_label == "Legal-Agent" ~ public_share + 0.020,
      agent_label == "PR-Agent" ~ public_share + 0.030,
      agent_label == "Social-Manager-Agent" ~ public_share + 0.018,
      agent_label == "PR-Intern-Agent" ~ public_share - 0.020,
      agent_label == "Intern-Agent" ~ public_share + 0.020,
      TRUE ~ public_share + 0.015
    )
  )

ggplot(
  bridge_data,
  aes(
    x = internal_share,
    y = public_share
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      size = total_messages,
      fill = bridge_score
    ),
    shape = 21,
    colour = "grey35",
    alpha = 0.38,
    stroke = 0.5
  ) +

  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = internal_share,
      y = public_share,
      xend = label_x,
      yend = label_y
    ),
    colour = "grey55",
    linewidth = 0.3,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +

  geom_label(
    aes(
      x = label_x,
      y = label_y,
      label = agent_label
    ),
    size = 3,
    label.size = 0.15,
    label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines"),
    fill = alpha("white", 0.82)
  ) +

  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    breaks = seq(0.45, 0.85, 0.05)
  ) +

  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    breaks = seq(0.00, 0.25, 0.05)
  ) +

  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0.45, 0.85),
    ylim = c(-0.015, 0.26),
    clip = "off"
  ) +

  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(3, 12)
  ) +

  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "lightblue",
    high = "darkblue"
  ) +

  labs(
    title = "Communication Boundary Bridge Map",
    subtitle = "Zoomed view of agents' internal and public communication shares",
    x = "Internal Communication Share",
    y = "Public Communication Share",
    size = "Total Messages",
    fill = "Bridge Score"
  ) +

  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.margin = margin(10, 50, 10, 10)
  )









This bridge map shows that PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent have the highest public communication shares, while Legal-Agent, PR-Agent, Social-Manager-Agent, and Platform-Trust-Agent are more embedded in internal communication. Platform-Trust-Agent corresponds to the larger bubble in the lower-right area, while Judge-Agent corresponds to the smaller nearby bubble. Agents positioned between internal and public communication spaces are important for later leak-tracing analysis because they may act as communication boundary bridges.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.6 Merger-Related Communication Concentration
This visual focuses only on communications containing merger-related terms. The mosaic-style chart shows both the relative volume of merger-related communications by agent and how those communications are distributed across internal, private, and public scopes.


Code
merger_mosaic_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(contains_merger == TRUE) %>%
  count(agent_label, communication_scope, name = "message_count") %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    agent_total = sum(message_count),
    scope_share = message_count / agent_total
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

agent_widths <- merger_mosaic_data %>%
  distinct(agent_label, agent_total) %>%
  arrange(desc(agent_total)) %>%
  mutate(
    width = agent_total / sum(agent_total),
    xmin = lag(cumsum(width), default = 0),
    xmax = cumsum(width)
  )

merger_mosaic_plot <- merger_mosaic_data %>%
  left_join(agent_widths, by = c("agent_label", "agent_total")) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  arrange(communication_scope, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    ymin = lag(cumsum(scope_share), default = 0),
    ymax = cumsum(scope_share),
    label_x = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
    label_y = (ymin + ymax) / 2
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(
  merger_mosaic_plot,
  aes(
    xmin = xmin,
    xmax = xmax,
    ymin = ymin,
    ymax = ymax,
    fill = communication_scope
  )
) +
  geom_rect(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = label_x,
      y = label_y,
      label = ifelse(message_count > 3, message_count, "")
    ),
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = agent_widths$xmin + agent_widths$width / 2,
    labels = agent_widths$agent_label,
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Merger-Related Communication Concentration",
    subtitle = "Column width shows each agent's merger-related volume; height shows scope composition",
    x = "Agent",
    y = "Share within Agent",
    fill = "Communication Scope"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1)
  )









This mosaic chart shows that merger-related communication is heavily concentrated among Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent, which have the widest columns. For both agents, most merger-related records are internal, but there is also a visible public component. PR-Intern-Agent has a smaller total volume, but a relatively large private share. This suggests that merger-related information was not limited to one actor or one communication scope, making these agents important for later leak-tracing analysis.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.7 Sensitive Signal Exposure by Agent
This visual compares how different agents were exposed to merger-related, confidentiality-related, and urgency-related communication signals. Unlike the previous visuals, which focus on structure and flow, this chart highlights risk-relevant content exposure by agent.


Code
sensitive_exposure <- communications_integrated %>%

agent_order <- sensitive_exposure %>%

sensitive_exposure <- sensitive_exposure %>%

ggplot(

) +

  ) +

Legal-Agent has the highest exposure across all three sensitive signals, especially merger- and urgency-related content. Social-Manager-Agent is also highly exposed to merger-related signals, while Platform-Trust-Agent stands out more on urgency-related content. Overall, sensitive information is concentrated among a few core agents rather than evenly distributed across the team.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
5.8 Embargo-Relevant Relationship Profile


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")

# Rebuild reply relationships for centrality measurement
reply_lookup <- communications_integrated %>%
  select(
    responding_to = message_id,
    source_agent = agent_label
  )

reply_links <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(!is.na(responding_to)) %>%
  left_join(
    reply_lookup,
    by = "responding_to"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(source_agent)) %>%
  mutate(
    target_agent = agent_label
  ) %>%
  filter(source_agent != target_agent)

reply_centrality <- bind_rows(
  reply_links %>%
    count(source_agent, name = "reply_links") %>%
    rename(agent_label = source_agent),
  
  reply_links %>%
    count(target_agent, name = "reply_links") %>%
    rename(agent_label = target_agent)
) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    reply_centrality = sum(reply_links),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Agent-level embargo relevance profile
agent_embargo_profile <- communications_integrated %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    total_messages = n(),
    
    pre6_merger = sum(
      date == as_date("2046-06-05") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time &
        contains_merger,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    pre6_public_merger = sum(
      date == as_date("2046-06-05") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time &
        is_public &
        contains_merger,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    public_share = mean(is_public, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    sensitive_exposure = sum(
      as.integer(contains_merger) +
        as.integer(contains_confidential) +
        as.integer(contains_urgency),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    reply_centrality,
    by = "agent_label"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    reply_centrality = replace_na(reply_centrality, 0)
  )

# Build communication boundary profile
boundary_profile <- communications_integrated %>%
  count(agent_label, communication_scope, name = "message_count") %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    total_scope_messages = sum(message_count),
    share = message_count / total_scope_messages
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(agent_label, communication_scope, share) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = communication_scope,
    values_from = share,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# Ensure expected communication scope columns exist
if (!"Internal" %in% names(boundary_profile)) {
  boundary_profile$Internal <- 0
}

if (!"Private / One-on-One" %in% names(boundary_profile)) {
  boundary_profile[["Private / One-on-One"]] <- 0
}

if (!"Public" %in% names(boundary_profile)) {
  boundary_profile$Public <- 0
}

boundary_profile <- boundary_profile %>%
  transmute(
    agent_label,
    internal_share = Internal,
    private_share = `Private / One-on-One`,
    public_scope_share = Public,
    boundary_bridge_score = private_share + public_scope_share
  )

agent_embargo_profile <- agent_embargo_profile %>%
  left_join(
    boundary_profile,
    by = "agent_label"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    boundary_bridge_score = replace_na(boundary_bridge_score, 0)
  )

# Convert metrics into long format and scale within each metric
embargo_profile_long <- agent_embargo_profile %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      pre6_merger,
      pre6_public_merger,
      public_share,
      boundary_bridge_score,
      sensitive_exposure,
      reply_centrality
    ),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "metric_value"
  ) %>%
  group_by(metric) %>%
  mutate(
    scaled_score = {
      metric_min <- min(metric_value, na.rm = TRUE)
      metric_max <- max(metric_value, na.rm = TRUE)
      
      if (is.infinite(metric_min) | is.infinite(metric_max) | metric_max == metric_min) {
        rep(0, n())
      } else {
        (metric_value - metric_min) / (metric_max - metric_min)
      }
    }
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      pre6_merger = "Pre-6PM Merger Activity",
      pre6_public_merger = "Pre-6PM Public Merger",
      public_share = "Public-Facing Share",
      boundary_bridge_score = "Boundary Bridge Score",
      sensitive_exposure = "Sensitive Signal Exposure",
      reply_centrality = "Reply Centrality"
    ),
    
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c(
        "Pre-6PM Merger Activity",
        "Pre-6PM Public Merger",
        "Public-Facing Share",
        "Boundary Bridge Score",
        "Sensitive Signal Exposure",
        "Reply Centrality"
      )
    ),
    
    label = case_when(
      metric %in% c("Public-Facing Share", "Boundary Bridge Score") ~
        scales::percent(metric_value, accuracy = 1),
      TRUE ~ as.character(round(metric_value, 0))
    )
  )

agent_order <- embargo_profile_long %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    total_score = sum(scaled_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(total_score) %>%
  pull(agent_label)

embargo_profile_long <- embargo_profile_long %>%
  mutate(
    agent_label = factor(agent_label, levels = agent_order)
  )

ggplot(
  embargo_profile_long,
  aes(
    x = metric,
    y = agent_label,
    fill = scaled_score
  )
) +
  geom_tile(
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    size = 3.1
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "white",
    high = "darkred"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Embargo-Relevant Relationship Profile",
    subtitle = "Agent-level comparison of pre-embargo merger activity, public exposure, sensitivity, and reply centrality",
    x = "Embargo-Relevant Dimension",
    y = "Agent",
    fill = "Relative Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )









Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent stand out as the most embargo-relevant actors because they combine high pre-6PM merger activity with strong sensitive-signal exposure. Platform-Trust-Agent is important through reply centrality and boundary relevance, suggesting a coordination role. PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent show stronger public-facing exposure, which makes them important for tracing how merger-related information could move toward public channels before the 6:00 PM embargo lift.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
section: 5.9 Key Findings from Communication Flow Analysis
text:
5.9 Key Findings from Communication Flow Analysis

Communication was concentrated around a core coordination group.
The reply-based flow and network graphs show that Legal-Agent, Platform-Trust-Agent, Social-Manager-Agent, and PR-Agent formed the main communication backbone. These agents were central to information exchange before the breach, which means that merger-related risk was managed through a small group of highly connected coordinators rather than through a fully isolated legal channel.
Merger-related information was not fully contained within legal control.
Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent had the highest pre-6PM merger activity and sensitive-signal exposure, but merger-related content also appeared across other agents, scopes, and channels. This suggests that confidential merger information had moved beyond a narrow legal-review context before the official embargo lift.
Public-facing boundary actors created potential release pathways.
PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent had higher public-facing shares, while Social-Manager-Agent connected internal coordination with public-facing communication. This matters because these agents sat closer to the boundary between internal information and public release, making them important for understanding how sensitive information could move from internal discussion toward public-facing spaces.
The embargo-relevant profile highlights different risk roles.
Legal-Agent and Social-Manager-Agent were most important for merger and sensitive-content exposure; Platform-Trust-Agent was important as a reply-centrality and coordination node; PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent were important because of their public-facing exposure. These roles indicate that the breach pathway was distributed across legal, monitoring, coordination, and public-facing functions.
Overall, the communication structure supports an internal-leak-enabled system failure interpretation.
Part 5 does not identify the original source of the Slack screenshot or prove that a senior agent deliberately leaked the merger. Instead, the graphs show the communication environment that made the breach difficult to contain: sensitive merger information circulated through core coordinators while public-facing boundary actors remained active before the embargo lift. Therefore, the network evidence should be read together with the Slack timeline from Part 4. The Slack screenshot provides the direct internal-leak evidence, while the Part 5 communication-flow visuals explain how that leak could be amplified through a fragmented multi-agent communication system.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
6.1 Purpose of Causal Event Analysis
The purpose of this section is to move from descriptive patterns to causal explanation. Earlier sections established that communication volume, merger-related discussion, public-facing exposure, and pressure signals all intensified before the embargo breach. However, those findings alone do not explain how the inappropriate release happened.
This section therefore reconstructs the event-level pathway that led to the pre-6:00 PM release of merger-related information. It focuses on three questions:

Which key actions and decision points appeared before the embargo lift?
Which agents were involved in those decisions or actions?
Which system elements allowed merger-related content to move from internal or private communication into public-facing channels?

The analysis is especially focused on the period before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift on June 5. Records involving merger-related content, decision/action language, public-facing communication, and enforcement-related signals are treated as key evidence for reconstructing the causal chain.
This section does not assume that the release was either deliberate or accidental at the outset. Instead, it evaluates whether the event pattern looks like a controlled intentional leak by a specific actor, or a broader system breakdown in which sensitive information passed through multiple agents, channels, and weak control points before reaching public communication.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
6.2 Condensed Key Event Sequence
This section condenses the communication records into a small number of causal stages. The purpose is not to repeat the full timeline analysis, but to show the main pathway from internal merger circulation to public-facing exposure before and after the embargo lift.


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")

causal_event_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  mutate(
    event_text = str_to_lower(content),

    causal_stage = case_when(
      contains_merger &
        !is_public &
        timestamp < breach_time ~
        "Internal merger circulation",

      contains_merger &
        str_detect(event_text, "urgent|asap|deadline|pressure|crisis|escalate|critical|risk") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Merger pressure escalation",

      contains_merger &
        str_detect(event_text, "embargo|confidential|restricted|sensitive|not public|internal only") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Confidentiality boundary present",

      str_detect(event_text, "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Decision / release action",

      str_detect(event_text, "hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Review / control attempt",

      str_detect(event_text, "judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy") &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Enforcement reference",

      is_public &
        contains_merger &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~
        "Public merger exposure before embargo lift",

      is_public &
        contains_merger &
        timestamp >= embargo_lift_time ~
        "Public merger release after embargo lift",

      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(causal_stage))

causal_stage_summary <- causal_event_data %>%
  group_by(causal_stage) %>%
  summarise(
    event_count = n(),
    agents_involved = n_distinct(agent_label),
    public_events = sum(is_public, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    stage_number = case_when(
      causal_stage == "Internal merger circulation" ~ 1,
      causal_stage == "Merger pressure escalation" ~ 2,
      causal_stage == "Confidentiality boundary present" ~ 3,
      causal_stage == "Decision / release action" ~ 4,
      causal_stage == "Review / control attempt" ~ 5,
      causal_stage == "Enforcement reference" ~ 6,
      causal_stage == "Public merger exposure before embargo lift" ~ 7,
      causal_stage == "Public merger release after embargo lift" ~ 8
    ),

    stage_group = case_when(
      causal_stage == "Internal merger circulation" ~ "Information Flow",
      causal_stage %in% c(
        "Merger pressure escalation",
        "Confidentiality boundary present"
      ) ~ "Pressure / Boundary",
      causal_stage %in% c(
        "Decision / release action",
        "Review / control attempt",
        "Enforcement reference"
      ) ~ "Decision / Control",
      causal_stage %in% c(
        "Public merger exposure before embargo lift",
        "Public merger release after embargo lift"
      ) ~ "Public Exposure"
    ),

    stage_label = paste0(stage_number, ". ", causal_stage),
    stage_label = str_wrap(stage_label, width = 32),
    stage_label = factor(stage_label, levels = rev(stage_label)),

    detail_label = paste0(
      event_count, " events",
      " | ", agents_involved, " agents",
      " | ", public_events, " public"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(stage_number)

ggplot(
  causal_stage_summary,
  aes(
    x = event_count,
    y = stage_label,
    fill = stage_group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.62,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(size = agents_involved),
    shape = 21,
    fill = "white",
    colour = "grey25",
    stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = detail_label),
    hjust = -0.05,
    size = 3.4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.35))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Information Flow" = "#4E79A7",
      "Pressure / Boundary" = "#F28E2B",
      "Decision / Control" = "#B07AA1",
      "Public Exposure" = "#E15759"
    )
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(3.5, 8),
    name = "Agents involved"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Condensed Key Event Sequence",
    subtitle = "Causal stages from internal merger circulation to public exposure",
    x = "Number of Events",
    y = "Causal Stage",
    fill = "Stage Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11)
  )









The chart summarises the breach pathway across eight causal stages. Decision/release action and review/control attempt have the largest event volumes, showing that action and control signals were both active before the embargo lift. However, public merger exposure still appeared before 6:00 PM, meaning that existing control and enforcement activity did not stop merger-related information from reaching public-facing communication.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
6.3 Decision and Control Failure Points
This section focuses only on the key decision and control nodes that were directly relevant to the embargo failure: approval or release actions, hold or review controls, enforcement references, and public merger exposure before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift.


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")

decision_control_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  mutate(
    event_text = str_to_lower(replace_na(content, "")),
    
    breach_phase = case_when(
      date < as_date("2046-06-05") ~ "Before June 5",
      date == as_date("2046-06-05") & timestamp < breach_time ~ "June 5 Before 5PM",
      date == as_date("2046-06-05") &
        timestamp >= breach_time &
        timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~ "5–6PM Breach Window",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    approval_release = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release"
    ) & timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
    
    hold_review = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready"
    ) & timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
    
    enforcement_reference = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy"
    ) & timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
    
    public_merger_exposure = is_public &
      contains_merger &
      timestamp < embargo_lift_time
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(breach_phase)) %>%
  mutate(
    breach_phase = factor(
      breach_phase,
      levels = c(
        "Before June 5",
        "June 5 Before 5PM",
        "5–6PM Breach Window"
      )
    )
  )

decision_control_summary <- decision_control_data %>%
  summarise(
    `Approval / release action` = sum(approval_release, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Hold / review control` = sum(hold_review, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Enforcement reference` = sum(enforcement_reference, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Public merger exposure before 6PM` = sum(public_merger_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = breach_phase
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -breach_phase,
    names_to = "control_node",
    values_to = "event_count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    control_node = factor(

      levels = c(

        "Hold / review control",
        "Enforcement reference",

  )

ggplot(

  aes(
    x = breach_phase,
    y = event_count,
    fill = control_node
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = event_count),
    vjust = -0.4,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ control_node,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Approval / release action" = "#4E79A7",
      "Hold / review control" = "#F28E2B",
      "Enforcement reference" = "#B07AA1",
      "Public merger exposure before 6PM" = "#E15759"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Decision and Control Failure Points",
    subtitle = "Key approval, hold, enforcement, and public-exposure nodes across the pre-embargo phases",
    x = "Pre-Embargo Phase",
    y = "Event Count",
    fill = "Control Node"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),

The chart shows that approval/release actions and hold/review controls were already active before the breach window, especially on June 5 before 5PM. However, public merger exposure also appeared before 6PM, with 9 cases before 5PM and 7 more during the 5–6PM breach window. This indicates that the problem was not the absence of decision or control activity, but the failure of those controls to stop merger-related information from reaching public-facing communication.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
6.4 Embargo Enforcement Failure Pathway
This section summarises the causal pathway that allowed embargoed merger information to move from internal communication into public-facing exposure before the official embargo lift. The flow direction shows the causal sequence, while bubble size gives a visual indication of the evidence volume at each stage.


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")

event_text <- str_to_lower(replace_na(communications_integrated$content, ""))

pathway_nodes <- tibble(
  step = 1:5,
  x = c(1, 2.25, 3.5, 4.75, 6),
  y = 1,
  stage = c(
    "Internal merger\ncirculation",
    "Pressure +\nconfidentiality",
    "Decision / review /\nenforcement activity",
    "Public-facing\nboundary",
    "Pre-6PM public\nmerger exposure"
  ),
  stage_group = c(
    "Information Flow",
    "Pressure / Sensitivity",
    "Decision / Control",
    "Boundary Exposure",
    "Embargo Failure"
  ),
  value_type = c(
    "events",
    "events",
    "events",
    "agents",
    "events"
  ),
  value = c(
    sum(
      communications_integrated$contains_merger &
        !communications_integrated$is_public &
        communications_integrated$timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    sum(
      communications_integrated$contains_merger &
        (
          str_detect(event_text, "urgent|asap|deadline|pressure|crisis|escalate|critical|risk") |
            str_detect(event_text, "embargo|confidential|restricted|sensitive|not public|internal only")
        ) &
        communications_integrated$timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    sum(
      (
        str_detect(event_text, "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release") |
          str_detect(event_text, "hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready") |
          str_detect(event_text, "judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy")
      ) &
        communications_integrated$timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    
    n_distinct(
      communications_integrated$agent_label[
        communications_integrated$is_public &
          communications_integrated$timestamp < embargo_lift_time
      ]
    ),
    
    sum(
      communications_integrated$is_public &
        communications_integrated$contains_merger &
        communications_integrated$timestamp < embargo_lift_time,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    display_size = scales::rescale(
      sqrt(value),
      to = c(10, 24)
    ),
    value_label = paste0(value, " ", value_type)
  )

pathway_edges <- pathway_nodes %>%
  arrange(step) %>%
  mutate(
    xend = lead(x),
    yend = lead(y)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(xend)) %>%
  mutate(
    x_start = x + 0.38,
    x_end = xend - 0.38
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = pathway_edges,
    aes(
      x = x_start,
      xend = x_end,
      y = y,
      yend = yend
    ),
    arrow = arrow(
      length = unit(0.25, "cm"),
      type = "closed"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.9,
    colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = pathway_nodes,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      fill = stage_group
    ),
    size = pathway_nodes$display_size,
    shape = 21,
    colour = "grey20",
    stroke = 0.9,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = pathway_nodes,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = 1.42,
      label = value_label
    ),
    size = 3.7,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = pathway_nodes,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = 0.45,
      label = stage
    ),
    size = 3.6,
    lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = pathway_nodes,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = 0.12,
      label = paste0("Step ", step)
    ),
    size = 3.2,
    colour = "grey35"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Information Flow" = "#4E79A7",
      "Pressure / Sensitivity" = "#F28E2B",
      "Decision / Control" = "#B07AA1",
      "Boundary Exposure" = "#59A14F",
      "Embargo Failure" = "#E15759"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0.45, 6.55),
    breaks = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1.65),
    breaks = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Embargo Enforcement Failure Pathway",
    subtitle = "Flow direction shows causal sequence; bubble size indicates relative evidence volume",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Pathway Stage"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20)
  )









This pathway summarises how the breach moved from internal merger circulation to public-facing exposure before the embargo lift. The key insight is that decision, review, and enforcement activity existed before the release, but those controls did not prevent merger-related information from crossing the public-facing boundary.

This evidence interpretation matrix shows that the strongest support is for internal leakage and system breakdown, rather than a proven senior-orchestrated leak. The Slack screenshot, the compromised information perimeter, and the Section 8.1 confidentiality issue all provide strong evidence that internal merger information reached the public domain before the authorised release. At the same time, the high scores under system breakdown show that the leak became serious because multiple agents, channels, and ineffective controls failed to contain the information under pressure. In contrast, the evidence for a senior-orchestrated leak remains weak or not proven, since no clear senior actor is identified as the original source. Overall, the matrix supports a mixed interpretation: the breach was an internal confidentiality leak enabled by system-level control failure, followed by deliberate post-leak crisis management.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
section: 6.6 Key Findings from Causal Chain Analysis
text:
6.6 Key Findings from Causal Chain Analysis

The inappropriate release followed a multi-stage pathway rather than a single isolated event.
Merger information first circulated internally, then became linked with pressure, confidentiality, decision/action, review/control, and enforcement-related activity before reaching public-facing exposure. This suggests that the breach developed through a sequence of escalating conditions rather than through one simple communication mistake.
The Slack screenshot provides direct evidence of internal leakage within the causal chain.
The causal pathway should not be interpreted as only external speculation or ordinary system pressure. The dataset records an employee Slack message stating that “the merger saves all our jobs” appearing on Said-it/r/PropTech, while Legal treated internal Slack screenshots reaching Said-it within about 20 minutes as a compromised information perimeter. This places a direct internal-leak event inside the causal chain.
Control activity was present, but it was not effective.
The decision/control analysis shows large volumes of approval/release actions and hold/review controls before the embargo lift. This means the problem was not a complete absence of review or enforcement, but a failure of those controls to prevent internal information from reaching public-facing spaces.
The breach became visible before the official 6:00 PM embargo lift.
Public merger exposure appeared before 6PM, including cases before 5PM and during the 5–6PM breach window. This confirms that the embargo boundary had already been crossed before the authorised release time.
The causal pathway involved multiple system layers.
The failure pathway shows internal merger circulation, pressure/confidentiality signals, decision/review/enforcement activity, public-facing boundary agents, and final pre-6PM public exposure. This indicates that the release was produced by interaction between an internal confidentiality breach and a weak multi-agent communication-control system.
The evidence supports internal leak plus system breakdown, rather than a clean binary conclusion.
The evidence matrix should not be read as proving either a purely accidental system breakdown or a fully deliberate senior-orchestrated leak. The Slack screenshot strongly supports the internal-leak interpretation, while the wider pattern of multiple agents, multiple channels, active but ineffective controls, and rising crisis pressure supports the system-breakdown interpretation. However, the available evidence does not clearly identify a single senior actor who deliberately planned the original leak. Therefore, the strongest causal conclusion is that the merger exposure resulted from an internal confidentiality leak enabled by system-level control failure, followed by deliberate post-leak crisis management.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.1 Purpose of Typical Behavior Comparison
The purpose of this section is to determine whether the behavior that led to the inappropriate release was consistent with prior system behavior or represented a meaningful deviation. Earlier sections reconstructed the breach timeline, communication relationships, and causal pathway. This section now compares the release-window behavior against the system’s typical behavior before June 5.
The analysis focuses on three questions:

What did normal communication behavior look like before the breach day?
How did the June 5 release-window behavior differ from that baseline?
Was pre-embargo public merger exposure a continuation of prior behavior, or a new and unusual pattern?

This comparison is important because a large number of leaked messages does not automatically prove deliberate intent. If the release-window behavior differs sharply from prior patterns across agents, channels, scopes, and message types, the evidence is more consistent with a system behavior shift under pressure. If the behavior had been common before, it would suggest that the breach was part of a recurring uncontrolled pattern rather than a new failure.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.2 Typical Communication Baseline Before June 5
This section establishes the typical communication baseline before the breach day. The purpose is to identify how agents normally behaved before June 5 across communication scope, merger-related content, public exposure, and decision/control language.


Code
baseline_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(date < as_date("2046-06-05")) %>%
  mutate(
    event_text = str_to_lower(replace_na(content, "")),
    
    decision_control_signal = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release|hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready|judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy"
    )
  )

baseline_agent_profile <- baseline_data %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    total_messages = n(),
    
    internal_share = mean(communication_scope == "Internal", na.rm = TRUE),
    private_share = mean(communication_scope == "Private / One-on-One", na.rm = TRUE),
    public_share = mean(communication_scope == "Public", na.rm = TRUE),
    
    merger_share = mean(contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    public_merger_share = mean(is_public & contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    decision_control_share = mean(decision_control_signal, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

baseline_heatmap_data <- baseline_agent_profile %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      internal_share,
      private_share,
      public_share,
      merger_share,
      public_merger_share,
      decision_control_share
    ),
    names_to = "baseline_metric",
    values_to = "metric_value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline_metric = recode(
      baseline_metric,
      internal_share = "Internal Communication",
      private_share = "Private / One-on-One",
      public_share = "Public Communication",
      merger_share = "Merger-Related Content",
      public_merger_share = "Public + Merger Content",
      decision_control_share = "Decision / Control Language"
    ),
    
    baseline_metric = factor(
      baseline_metric,
      levels = c(
        "Internal Communication",
        "Private / One-on-One",
        "Public Communication",
        "Merger-Related Content",
        "Public + Merger Content",
        "Decision / Control Language"
      )
    ),
    
    label = scales::percent(metric_value, accuracy = 1)
  )

agent_order_baseline <- baseline_heatmap_data %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    baseline_intensity = sum(metric_value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(baseline_intensity) %>%
  pull(agent_label)

baseline_heatmap_data <- baseline_heatmap_data %>%
  mutate(
    agent_label = factor(agent_label, levels = agent_order_baseline)
  )

ggplot(
  baseline_heatmap_data,
  aes(
    x = baseline_metric,
    y = agent_label,
    fill = metric_value
  )
) +
  geom_tile(
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "white",
    high = "darkred",
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Typical Communication Baseline Before June 5",
    subtitle = "Agent-level baseline across communication scope, merger content, and control language",
    x = "Baseline Behavior Metric",
    y = "Agent",
    fill = "Share of Messages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11)
  )









This baseline shows that before June 5, most agents mainly operated in internal or private communication spaces, while public communication was concentrated among PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent. Public + merger content was 0% across all agents, which is the most important baseline finding. This means that pre-embargo public merger exposure was not part of normal prior behavior, making the June 5 release-window behavior a clear deviation from the typical communication pattern.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.2 Typical Communication Baseline Before June 5
This section establishes the typical communication baseline before the breach day. The purpose is to identify how agents normally communicated before June 5 across communication scope, channel, and message type. This baseline provides the reference point for comparing whether the June 5 release-window behavior was a normal continuation of prior behavior or a meaningful deviation.


Code
baseline_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  filter(date < as_date("2046-06-05"))

baseline_scope <- baseline_data %>%
  count(
    agent_label,
    communication_scope,
    name = "message_count"
  ) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    share = message_count / sum(message_count),
    baseline_dimension = "Communication Scope",
    category = communication_scope
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

baseline_channel <- baseline_data %>%
  count(
    agent_label,
    channel,
    name = "message_count"
  ) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    share = message_count / sum(message_count),
    baseline_dimension = "Channel",
    category = channel
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

baseline_message_type <- baseline_data %>%
  count(
    agent_label,
    message_type,
    name = "message_count"
  ) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  mutate(
    share = message_count / sum(message_count),
    baseline_dimension = "Message Type",
    category = message_type
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

baseline_structure <- bind_rows(
  baseline_scope,
  baseline_channel,
  baseline_message_type
) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline_dimension = factor(
      baseline_dimension,
      levels = c(
        "Communication Scope",
        "Channel",
        "Message Type"
      )
    ),
    category = str_wrap(category, width = 18),
    label = ifelse(
      share >= 0.12,
      scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1),
      ""
    )
  )

agent_order_baseline <- baseline_data %>%
  count(agent_label, name = "total_messages") %>%
  arrange(total_messages) %>%
  pull(agent_label)

baseline_structure <- baseline_structure %>%
  mutate(
    agent_label = factor(agent_label, levels = agent_order_baseline)
  )

ggplot(
  baseline_structure,
  aes(
    x = agent_label,
    y = share,
    fill = category
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.72,
    colour = "white",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = label),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    size = 2.7,
    colour = "black"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ baseline_dimension,
    ncol = 1,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Typical Communication Baseline Before June 5",
    subtitle = "Pre-breach agent behavior across scope, channel, and message type",
    x = "Agent",
    y = "Share of Messages",
    fill = "Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11)
  )









This baseline shows that before June 5, agents had clearly different normal communication patterns. PR-Intern-Agent and Intern-Agent were the most public-facing, while Legal-Agent, Platform-Trust-Agent, Social-Manager-Agent, and Judge-Agent were mainly internal or private. The channel and message-type panels also show that core coordination agents relied more on comms_huddle, one_on_one_chat, and broadcast-style messages, while public-post behavior was concentrated in fewer boundary-facing agents. This baseline is important because it shows what “normal” looked like before comparing it with the June 5 release-window behavior.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.3 Release-Window Behavior Profile
This section compares each agent’s typical pre-June 5 behavior with its behavior during the 5–6PM breach window. The comparison focuses on four release-relevant indicators: public communication, merger-related content, public merger exposure, and decision/control language.


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")

behavior_comparison_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  mutate(
    event_text = str_to_lower(replace_na(content, "")),
    
    period = case_when(
      date < as_date("2046-06-05") ~ "Baseline before June 5",
      timestamp >= breach_time & timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~ "5–6PM breach window",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    decision_control_signal = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release|hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready|judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(period))

agent_behavior_profile <- behavior_comparison_data %>%
  group_by(agent_label, period) %>%
  summarise(
    total_messages = n(),
    public_share = mean(is_public, na.rm = TRUE),
    merger_share = mean(contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    public_merger_share = mean(is_public & contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    decision_control_share = mean(decision_control_signal, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

all_agents <- sort(unique(communications_integrated$agent_label))

agent_behavior_profile <- tidyr::complete(
  agent_behavior_profile,
  agent_label = all_agents,
  period = c("Baseline before June 5", "5–6PM breach window"),
  fill = list(
    total_messages = 0,
    public_share = 0,
    merger_share = 0,
    public_merger_share = 0,
    decision_control_share = 0
  )
)

behavior_long <- agent_behavior_profile %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      public_share,
      merger_share,
      public_merger_share,
      decision_control_share
    ),
    names_to = "behavior_metric",
    values_to = "share"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    behavior_metric = recode(

Decision/control language remains high for several core agents, which suggests that the release-window behavior changed under active control pressure rather than in the absence of controls.

title: Take-Home_Ex02
text:
7.4 Behavioral Deviation Score by Agent
This section aggregates the release-window behavioral shifts into an agent-level deviation profile. Each radar panel shows how much an agent’s 5–6PM breach-window behavior deviated from its pre-June 5 baseline across four release-relevant dimensions.


Code
embargo_lift_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00")
breach_time <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00")

deviation_data <- communications_integrated %>%
  mutate(
    event_text = str_to_lower(replace_na(content, "")),
    
    period = case_when(
      date < as_date("2046-06-05") ~ "Baseline before June 5",
      timestamp >= breach_time & timestamp < embargo_lift_time ~ "5–6PM breach window",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    
    decision_control_signal = str_detect(
      event_text,
      "approve|approval|greenlight|go ahead|clearance|execute|publish|post|release|hold|wait|pause|review|monitor|block|do not|don't|cannot|not ready|judge|enforcement|guardrail|compliance|policy"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(period))

agent_deviation_profile <- deviation_data %>%
  group_by(agent_label, period) %>%
  summarise(
    public_share = mean(is_public, na.rm = TRUE),
    merger_share = mean(contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    public_merger_share = mean(is_public & contains_merger, na.rm = TRUE),
    decision_control_share = mean(decision_control_signal, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::complete(
    agent_label,
    period = c("Baseline before June 5", "5–6PM breach window"),
    fill = list(
      public_share = 0,
      merger_share = 0,
      public_merger_share = 0,
      decision_control_share = 0
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      public_share,
      merger_share,
      public_merger_share,
      decision_control_share
    ),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "share"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = share
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    deviation = abs(`5–6PM breach window` - `Baseline before June 5`),
    
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      public_share = "Public\nCommunication",
      merger_share = "Merger\nContent",
      public_merger_share = "Public +\nMerger",
      decision_control_share = "Decision /\nControl"
    ),
    
    metric = factor(
      metric,
      levels = c(
        "Public\nCommunication",
        "Merger\nContent",
        "Public +\nMerger",
        "Decision /\nControl"
      )
    )
  )

agent_deviation_score <- agent_deviation_profile %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  summarise(
    deviation_score = sum(deviation, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(deviation_score))

agent_deviation_profile <- agent_deviation_profile %>%
  left_join(agent_deviation_score, by = "agent_label") %>%
  mutate(
    agent_label = factor(
      agent_label,
      levels = rev(agent_deviation_score$agent_label)
    )
  )

# Scale all deviations to the same 0–1 range for radar plotting
max_deviation <- max(agent_deviation_profile$deviation, na.rm = TRUE)

radar_data <- agent_deviation_profile %>%
  mutate(
    scaled_deviation = if (is.na(max_deviation) | max_deviation == 0) {
      0
    } else {
      deviation / max_deviation
    },
    
    metric_id = as.integer(metric),
    angle = 2 * pi * (metric_id - 1) / nlevels(metric),
    x = scaled_deviation * sin(angle),
    y = scaled_deviation * cos(angle),
    
    label_x = 1.18 * sin(angle),
    label_y = 1.18 * cos(angle),
    
    value_label = ifelse(
      deviation > 0,
      scales::percent(deviation, accuracy = 1),
      ""
    )
  )

# Close each radar polygon
radar_polygon_data <- radar_data %>%
  arrange(agent_label, metric_id) %>%
  group_by(agent_label) %>%
  bind_rows(slice(., 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Radar grid
grid_levels <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)

radar_grid <- expand_grid(
  grid_level = grid_levels,
  metric_id = 1:nlevels(radar_data$metric)
) %>%
  mutate(
    angle = 2 * pi * (metric_id - 1) / nlevels(radar_data$metric),
    x = grid_level * sin(angle),
    y = grid_level * cos(angle)
  ) %>%
  group_by(grid_level) %>%
  bind_rows(slice(., 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

radar_axes <- tibble(
  metric = levels(radar_data$metric),
  metric_id = 1:nlevels(radar_data$metric)
) %>%
  mutate(
    angle = 2 * pi * (metric_id - 1) / nlevels(radar_data$metric),
    x = sin(angle),
    y = cos(angle),
    label_x = 1.08 * sin(angle),
    label_y = 1.08 * cos(angle)
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_path(
    data = radar_grid,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      group = grid_level
    ),
    colour = "grey82",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = radar_axes,
    aes(
      x = 0,
      y = 0,
      xend = x,
      yend = y
    ),
    colour = "grey78",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = radar_polygon_data,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      group = agent_label
    ),
    fill = "#E15759",
    alpha = 0.25,
    colour = "#E15759",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = radar_data,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y
    ),
    colour = "#E15759",
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = radar_data,
    aes(
      x = x,
      y = y,
      label = value_label
    ),
    size = 2.7,
    vjust = -0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = radar_axes,
    aes(
      x = label_x,
      y = label_y,
      label = metric
    ),
    size = 2.3,
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ agent_label,
    ncol = 3
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "Behavioral Deviation Profile by Agent",
    subtitle = "Radar panels show each agent's release-window deviation from baseline behavior",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 15, 10, 15)
  )











Code
agent_deviation_score %>%
  mutate(
    `Deviation Score` = round(deviation_score, 3)
  ) %>%
  select(
    Agent = agent_label,
    `Deviation Score`
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
